ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethical Review Board at SWPS University.
Ninety-three university students were recruited for course credit; two were excluded due to EMG recording failure, leaving N = 91 (65 women).
Participants were informed the study concerned user experience in video calls with one-or two-way visual access, and that their video signal might be viewed by senders.
Block order as well as trial order within blocks were randomized per participant.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Ninety-three university students were recruited for course credit; two were excluded due to EMG recording failure, leaving N = 91 (65 women).

> Participants were informed the study concerned user experience in video calls with one-or two-way visual access, and that their video signal might be viewed by senders.

> Block order as well as trial order within blocks were randomized per participant.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study was approved by the Ethical Review Board at SWPS University.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The study used a 2 (Modality: bimodal vs. vocal-only) × 2 (Self-Camera: on vs. off) × 4 (Emotion: anger, disgust, sadness, happiness) within-participants design. Ninety-three university students were recruited for course credit; two were excluded due to EMG recording failure, leaving N = 91 (65 women). Monte Carlo power simulations (simr, 1000 iterations) confirmed >80% power for fixed effects of β = 0.04-0.06 (full details at OSF).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: sample_size, alpha_level ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "unknown", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = NA_real_, alpha_level = NA_real_, power = 0.8, effect_size = 0.04, effect_size_metric = "other", software = "simr"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "The study used a 2 (Modality: bimodal vs. vocal-only) × 2 (Self-Camera: on vs. off) × 4 (Emotion: anger, disgust, sadness, happiness) within-participants design. Ninety-three university students were recruited for course credit; two were excluded due to EMG recording failure, leaving N = 91 (65 women). Monte Carlo power simulations (simr, 1000 iterations) confirmed >80% power for fixed effects of β = 0.04-0.06 (full details at OSF)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps ≤ .004", "ps ≥ .157", "ps ≥ .439", 
"ps ≥ .294"), Text = c("Anger was rated as more intense than all other displays (Disgust: d = 0.19; Sadness: d = 0.27; Happiness: d = 0.34; all ps ≤ .004; F(3, 115) = 14.42, p < .001, η² = 0.27).", 
"Remaining interactions were non-significant (ps ≥ .157).", 
"Remaining interactions were non-significant (ps ≥ .439).", 
"All remaining interactions were non-significant (ps ≥ .294)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 101 columns across 6 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Knowing You Seeing Me: The Role of Visual Contact During Video-Conferencing for Emotion Recognition and Mimicry

author.affiliation:
Center for Research on Biological Basis of Social Behavior
								SWPS University
								
									Warsaw
									Poland

Center for Research on Biological Basis of Social Behavior
								SWPS University
								
									Warsaw
									Poland

text.text: This study investigated how asymmetrical visual access in video-conferencing-specifically sender and receiver camera status-affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry.
Ninetyone participants viewed bimodal (facial-vocal) or vocal-only displays of four emotions (anger, disgust, sadness, and happiness) while their own camera was either on or off.
Recognition accuracy, intensity ratings, and facial muscle activity (EMG) were recorded.
Results revealed that bimodal displays significantly enhanced recognition accuracy and perceived intensity compared to vocal-only signals, except for sadness.
Emotional mimicry was most pronounced for affiliative displays (happiness and sadness) and was significantly stronger in the bimodal condition.
Exploratory analyses suggested that the awareness of being observed (self-camera on) intensified smile-like reactions and improved the recognition of sadness.
These findings suggest that mutual visibility facilitates emotion recognition and affiliative mimicry.
The self-camera may function as a cue for public self-awareness, possibly sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor's emotional signals.
This research highlights the importance of multimodal communication in sustaining interpersonal synchronization during remote interactions.
The growing prevalence of videoconferencing makes understanding its impact on emotional communication increasingly critical.

Unlike face-to-face interaction, videoconferencing creates asymmetric visual access -a sender's disabled camera renders their facial expressions invisible, while a receiver's camera-off status deprives the sender of engagement feedback -introducing challenges for nonverbal cue exchange, cognitive load, and fatigue. [1] [2] [3] Nonverbal cues -facial displays, vocal expressions, and gaze -are central to emotional communication, supporting inference of others' states, behavioral prediction, and emotional synchronization between partners. [4] [5] [6] [7] Evidence on whether videoconferencing preserves these functions is mixed: while some studies report synchrony, trust, and interaction quality comparable to face-to-face contact, [8] [9] [10] [11] reduced visual access has been linked to lower mutual understanding. 12, 13 This is consistent with broader emotion recognition research showing multimodal stimuli are recognized more accurately than audio-only signals, 14, 15 suggesting that diminished mutual understanding under camera-off conditions may partly reflect the loss of this multimodal advantage.

text.text: Visual contact is shaped not only by the sender's camera status, but also by the receiver's own.
Activating one's camera heightens public self-awareness -increasing sensitivity to one's observability -promoting affiliative signaling and expressive regulation.

At the same time, camera activation typically triggers self-view, which may capture attentional resources and impair processing of the partner's signals. 2, 18 Camera activation thus engages two partially dissociable processes: public self-awareness, promoting affiliative behavior, and self-focused attention, introducing potential attentional costs.

text.text: These conditions are particularly relevant for emotional mimicry -the tendency to imitate another person's emotional display 19 -a key mechanism not yet extensively studied in videoconferencing contexts.
text.formatted: These conditions are particularly relevant for emotional mimicry -the tendency to imitate another person's emotional display <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> -a key mechanism not yet extensively studied in videoconferencing contexts.

text.text: Mimicry is stronger for affiliative displays (happiness, sadness) than for antagonistic ones (anger, disgust 20, 21 ), is modulated by social context and attentional focus, 22, 23 and functionally supports affiliative outcomes and impression formation. 5, 19, 24, 25 Although facial mimicry can be elicited by vocal expressions alone, [26] [27] [28] vocal-only signals may yield weaker responses than multimodal ones, 29 suggesting that camera-off conditions impair both mimicry and related social inference processes. 30 The present study examined how multimodal emotional signals (facial-vocal vs. vocalonly) and receiver camera status jointly affect emotion recognition and facial mimicry.

text.text: We hypothesized that bimodal displays would enhance recognition accuracy, perceived intensity, and mimicry.
Awareness of being seen was expected to promote affiliative regulation, improving sadness recognition and amplifying smile-like mimicry, with minimal mimicry for antagonistic displays.
The study was approved by the Ethical Review Board at SWPS University.
Materials, data, and analysis scripts are available at OSF (https://osf.io/usgm3/).
text.formatted: Materials, data, and analysis scripts are available at OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/usgm3/">https://osf.io/usgm3/</ref>).

text.text: The study used a 2 (Modality: bimodal vs. vocal-only) × 2 (Self-Camera: on vs. off) × 4 (Emotion: anger, disgust, sadness, happiness) within-participants design.
Ninety-three university students were recruited for course credit; two were excluded due to EMG recording failure, leaving N = 91 (65 women).
Monte Carlo power simulations (simr, 1000 iterations) confirmed >80% power for fixed effects of β = 0.04-0.06 (full details at OSF).
text.formatted: Monte Carlo power simulations (simr, 1000 iterations) confirmed >80% power for fixed effects of β = 0.04-0.06 (full details at OSF).

text.text: Stimuli consisted of 16 short clips (2-5 s) of emotional displays produced by six professional actors (3F, 3M), extracted from longer speech samples in which actors addressed a hypothetical interlocutor as in a simulated video call.
An initial pool of stimuli was prescreened by independent judges, yielding 104 clips meeting technical criteria (e.g., minimum 2-s duration, neutral facial expression at onset and offset).
These clips were then rated by over 600 participants in a short Qualtrics survey, each viewing 26 randomly assigned recordings on intensity and authenticity (1 = low,5 = high).
For each emotion, the four clips with the highest authenticity ratings were selected as experimental stimuli (stimulus details at OSF).
Facial mimicry was measured using fEMG electrodes placed over the left zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii; depressor anguli oris and levator labii superioris.
The signal was digitized at 2 kHz, bandpass filtered (20-400 Hz), notch filtered (50 Hz), rectified, and baseline-corrected (0.5 s pre-stimulus).

Residual correlations confirmed moderate-to-strong cross-talk among lower-face muscles 31 (rs = 0.46-0.54) and high selectivity of corrugator (rs ≤ 0.09; Table 1); analyses were therefore limited to zygomaticus and corrugator.
text.formatted: Residual correlations confirmed moderate-to-strong cross-talk among lower-face muscles <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">31</ref> (rs = 0.46-0.54) and high selectivity of corrugator (rs ≤ 0.09; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>); analyses were therefore limited to zygomaticus and corrugator.

text.text: Nonresponders (signal variability < 5% from baseline; Zygomaticus: n = 2; Corrugator: n = 1) and artifacts (±3 SD; < 1.5% of data points) were excluded; remaining data were re-standardized per-participant, baseline-corrected, and averaged across trials.
text.formatted: Nonresponders (signal variability < 5% from baseline; Zygomaticus: n = 2; Corrugator: n = 1) and artifacts (±3 SD; < 1.5% of data points) were excluded; remaining data were re-standardized per-participant, baseline-corrected, and averaged across trials.

text.text: Participants were informed the study concerned user experience in video calls with one-or two-way visual access, and that their video signal might be viewed by senders.

Four blocks of 16 trials (each emotion was represented by four clips, not all featuring the same actors) were presented in random order, each reflecting one Modality × Self-Camera combination (64 trials total).
Block order as well as trial order within blocks were randomized per participant.

Each trial began with a 3-s fixation cross, followed by a 3-s screen simulating a browser-based video call interface (camera status icons, muted microphone), after which the emotional display was presented.
To prevent self-focused attention, no video signal was transmitted back to participants.

Following a 5-s blank screen, participants categorized the emotion (i.e.: happiness, anger, disgust, sadness, fear, surprise, or other) and rated its intensity (1-5 scale: low -high); both responses were self-paced, with no time limit imposed.
Figure 1 illustrates example screens. the condition in which both the participant's and the sender's cameras were on.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> illustrates example screens. the condition in which both the participant's and the sender's cameras were on.

text.text: A screen informing the participant that the camera was active was displayed for 3 seconds and was followed by the video presentation.
The camera status icon indicated that the camera was on.
The lower panel shows the condition in which both cameras were off.

All analyses used mixed-effects modeling in R (lme4, lmerTest): Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM; binomial distribution, logit link) for emotion recognition accuracy and Linear Mixed Models (LMM; REML estimation, Type III tests with Satterthwaite's approximation) for intensity ratings and EMG activation.

Following Barr et al., 32 maximal random-effects structures, including random intercepts and slopes for Participant ID (Display, Modality, Self-Camera) and Actor ID (Display, Modality) were specified.
text.formatted: Following Barr et al., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32</ref> maximal random-effects structures, including random intercepts and slopes for Participant ID (Display, Modality, Self-Camera) and Actor ID (Display, Modality) were specified.

text.text: Models were simplified stepwise in cases of convergence failure or singular fit, by removing near-zero variance slopes, random effect correlations.
Recognition accuracy was re-coded as correct (1) vs. incorrect (0), with sum-to-zero contrasts for fixed effects.
The final model retained random slopes for Display and Modality across Participant (conditional R² = .51, marginal R² = .06).
Overall accuracy was very high (M = 93%; OR = 51, B = 3.94).
The main effect of Display was non-significant (χ²(3) = 6.65, p = .083), though anger was recognized more accurately than sadness (OR = 2.33, p = .066).
Modality was significant (χ²(1) = 15.42, p < .001): bimodal displays were over twice as likely to be correctly recognized than vocal-only (OR = 2.17).
text.formatted: Modality was significant (χ²(1) = 15.42, p < .001): bimodal displays were over twice as likely to be correctly recognized than vocal-only (OR = 2.17).

text.text: Self-Camera had no main effect (χ²(1) = 2.25, p = .133).

Crucially, a significant Display × Modality interaction (χ²(3) = 17.20, p < .001) revealed that bimodal advantage was significant for Disgust (OR = 5.75, p < .001) and Happiness (OR = 1.98, p = .027), marginal for Anger (OR = 2.04, p = .053), and absent for Sadness (OR = 0.95, p = .856).

text.text: The Display × Self-Camera interaction was non-significant (χ²(3) = 6.57, p = .087); exploratory follow-up simple effects nonetheless suggested that sadness recognition was less accurate when self-camera was off vs. on (OR = 0.54, p = .003).

Happiness elicited the strongest corrugator deactivation relative to all other displays (ds = 0.66-0.96, all ps < .001; F(3, 109) = 52.47, p < .001, η² = 0.59), while Sadness evoked greater activation than Anger (d = 0.30, p < .001) and Disgust (d = 0.20, p = .003).

Remaining interactions were non-significant (ps ≥ .439).

Bayesian mediation analyses (brms 33 ) tested whether a mimicry congruence index (Zygomaticus minus Corrugator, reversed for negative emotions) mediated the effect of affiliative potential of emotional display (i.e.: anger < disgust < sadness < happiness) 34 on recognition accuracy and intensity ratings.

text.text: As can be seen in Table 2 the indirect effect for recognition included zero; for intensity it was credibly non-zero but very small and opposite in sign to the direct effect (inconsistent mediation), so these results are exploratory.

text.text: The present study examined how asymmetric visual access during video calls affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry.
Bimodal displays were recognized more accurately and rated as more intense than vocal-only -except for sadness, for which no bimodal advantage emerged.

Mimicry was strongest for affiliative displays (happiness, sadness) and stronger for bimodal than vocal-only stimuli; exploratory analyses suggested larger smile-like responses and better sadness recognition when self-camera was on.
Mimicry-congruent muscle activation had only a small, inconsistent indirect association with perceived intensity and none with recognition accuracy, likely due to a ceiling effect.
These findings implicate that combined facial and vocal signals provide a richer social context, facilitating emotion decoding and affiliative mimicry.
The self-camera effects on sadness recognition and smile mimicry stemmed from interactions that only approached conventional significance and should be treated as exploratory.

With appropriate caution, the pattern is consistent with the Social Monitoring System framework, 35, 36 which predicts heightened sensitivity to prosocial cues when feeling observed -including distress signals such as sadness. 37, 38 Being seen by an interlocutor may "tune" this monitoring system toward socially demanding signals, such as sadness, that call for a supportive response.
text.formatted: With appropriate caution, the pattern is consistent with the Social Monitoring System framework, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">36</ref> which predicts heightened sensitivity to prosocial cues when feeling observed -including distress signals such as sadness. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">38</ref> Being seen by an interlocutor may "tune" this monitoring system toward socially demanding signals, such as sadness, that call for a supportive response.

text.text: The pronounced mimicry of affiliative displays under mutual visual contact is consistent with the view of mimicry as a social regulatory mechanism 19 which may enable a more nuanced, embodied understanding of an interlocutor's internal states, as evidenced by the mediation of smile mimicry on intensity ratings. 25 Together, these results offer initial support for the idea that that camera activation may engage public self-awareness as a social regulatory mechanism, 19 sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor's affiliative signals rather than acting merely as an attentional distractor.
text.formatted: The pronounced mimicry of affiliative displays under mutual visual contact is consistent with the view of mimicry as a social regulatory mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> which may enable a more nuanced, embodied understanding of an interlocutor's internal states, as evidenced by the mediation of smile mimicry on intensity ratings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> Together, these results offer initial support for the idea that that camera activation may engage public self-awareness as a social regulatory mechanism, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor's affiliative signals rather than acting merely as an attentional distractor.

text.text: Several limitations should be noted.
The use of brief, isolated emotional displaysnecessitated by fEMG requirements -limits ecological validity relative to real conversations.
The high accuracy may also partly reflect actors' clear, posed expressions, contributing to the ceiling effect.

Although stimuli were pre-selected for high perceived authenticity, they nonetheless portrayed professionally posed rather than spontaneous expressions, extracted outside a genuine conversational context.
Future studies should employ longer, naturalistic speech samples, enabling measures of emotional contagion and trait inferences.

Self-camera status was conveyed via a status icon without actual self-view; this comparatively weak manipulation, chosen to isolate public self-awareness from self-focused attention costs -but future studies should include real-time self-view conditions to fully disentangle these processes. 39 Several effects, though statistically significant given the large number of trials, were of limited practical significance.
text.formatted: Self-camera status was conveyed via a status icon without actual self-view; this comparatively weak manipulation, chosen to isolate public self-awareness from self-focused attention costs -but future studies should include real-time self-view conditions to fully disentangle these processes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">39</ref> Several effects, though statistically significant given the large number of trials, were of limited practical significance.

text.text: The predominantly female, student sample limits generalizability, and gender was not modeled as a factor.
As gender has been shown to modulate mimicry responses in other contexts, 40, 41 future studies would benefit from explicitly testing this factor.

Self-Camera had no main effect (p = .260).

A marginal Display × Self-Camera interaction (F(3, 5572) = 2.41, p = .064) was followed up with exploratory simple tentatively suggests that awareness of being seen may further modulate these processes.

Because participants never saw their own video, the study cannot address the attentional costs of self-view; it may, however, offer a counterweight to treating the self-camera solely as a distraction, suggesting that signaling visibility without a self-view window is worth testing.
Encouraging bimodal communication may help sustain the affiliative processes essential for mutual understanding in remote interactions.
